appraisal_events.evidence: « Vraiment ces gens sont sublimes de bourgeoisisme… ils doivent sortir du théâtre de Labiche ! » ; « Idiote, menteuse ! … et ça croit aimer l’Art ! » ; « maquerelle, entremetteuse ! » ; « Quelle gaîté fétide ! »
appraisal_events.explanation: Walking home, Swann delivers a sustained invective against Mme Verdurin and her salon, denouncing it as vulgar, stupid and ignoble. The narrator ironizes the whole tirade by dating its cause precisely — « maintenant que c’était un autre que lui qu’Odette allait y rencontrer… lui exhibait ses ridicules, sa sottise, son ignominie » — so the blame is staged as jealousy retro-fitted with morality rather than as an evaluation the passage underwrites.

appraisal_events.evidence: « sur le même ton un peu factice » ; « en relevant la tête, en redressant fièrement son corps en arrière » ; « comme si cette mission d’arracher Odette à une atmosphère de sarcasmes datait de plus longtemps que de quelques minutes, et comme s’il ne se l’était pas donnée seulement depuis qu’il pensait que ces sarcasmes l’avaient peut-être lui-même pour objet »
appraisal_events.explanation: The narrator directly punctures Swann's high moral posture, exposing his claim to inhabit an altitude above the Verdurins as a self-flattering fiction minutes old, invented once he suspected he was the joke's target. The same movement shows him displaced: Mme Verdurin will slip praise of Forcheville to Odette and seat him beside her in the dark, exactly as she once did for Swann.

status_effects.explanation: Swann is left talking aloud to himself in the Bois, convulsed with disgust and jealousy, imagining Odette laughing at him beside a rival; he has lost all leverage over the salon and over Odette's evening.
The narrator's exposure of the factitious tone and the just-invented rescue mission makes Swann's eloquence look like grandiloquent self-deception rather than discernment.
Forcheville takes over the place Swann is losing: invited by the painter with Odette, praised by Mme Verdurin, and installed at Odette's side during the music.
She is the sustained target of Swann's contempt as liar, hypocrite about art, and procuress; the diminishment is real but damped because the passage frames the verdict as jealousy speaking.

The same tirade sweeps Odette in — « car elle est si vulgaire et surtout, la pauvre petite, elle est tellement bête !!! » — a rare local downgrade of her by the man who idealizes her, though it too is coloured by his jealousy.

ambiguities: The contempt for the Verdurin salon is voiced by Swann but overlaps with judgments the narrative elsewhere lets stand; the passage marks the timing of Swann's reversal as suspect without clearly asserting that the salon is in fact estimable, so how far Mme Verdurin is genuinely diminished remains underdetermined.
